carouselA.title: The Institution Hidden Inside the Contract: the institutional sequence

frames.caption: A fashion contract does more than price a transaction: it assigns roles, approvals, rights, records, risk, credit, access, transition duties, and the rules that govern what happens when the relationship changes.

frames.caption: 01 · BEFORE — What enters the relationship?. Define parties, authority to sign, pre-existing materials, references, confidential inputs, third-party components, permissions, territory, intended channels, and the difference between background assets and new deliverables.

frames.caption: 02 · DURING — How does work move?. Specify deliverables, milestones, dependencies, review windows, named approvers, revision rounds, acceptance, change control, credit, documentation, source-file delivery, accessibility, and rights evidence. The schedule is a governance map.
frames.credit: Concept and editorial design: RN Collins
frames.alt: Diagram mapping how does work move? within The Institution Hidden Inside the Contract.

frames.caption: 03 · CONTROL — Who may do what with the result?. Separate ownership from license; identify exclusivity, fields of use, territory, term, sublicensing, modification, archive, publicity, moral-rights issues where applicable, and statutory work-made-for-hire or transfer requirements.
frames.credit: Concept and editorial design: RN Collins
frames.alt: Diagram mapping who may do what with the result? within The Institution Hidden Inside the Contract.
frames.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery
frames.treatment: render from verified text, source IDs, lines and geometric fields

frames.crop: native 4:5 diagram; preserve labels and evidence footer
frames.caption: 04 · AFTER — What survives change?. Map payment on termination, kill fees, return or deletion, archive copy, confidentiality, transition help, continuing licenses, credit correction, takedown, dispute procedure, and who retains the evidence needed to enforce or explain the deal.

frames.caption: Contract architecture can become extractive: the party with leverage can demand sweeping ownership, perpetual use, silence, and risk transfer. More clauses are not automatically fairer. The counterweight is proportionality, real negotiation, legible language, preserved versions, independent advice, and a record of whose labor and community knowledge the agreement affects.
frames.alt: Counterpoint card for The Institution Hidden Inside the Contract.
frames.treatment: typographic quotation field; no decorative imagery

frames.caption: Mark every approval, acceptance, revision, payment, credit, rights, access, and record obligation.
